About this manual

Thank you for choosing the Luchs A, an open, high-performance mobile robot chassis for research, development, prototyping and pilot projects.

This manual gives you complete and accurate information about the product and how to operate it. To use the chassis safely and get the best from it, please read this manual before you start, and keep it for future reference.

Who this manual is for

This manual covers the hardware architecture, low-level communication protocols, motion control and sensor integration. It is written mainly for:

  • Robotics and software engineers who develop higher-level algorithms, integrate systems or build product prototypes on the Luchs A, and need a detailed understanding of its interfaces, communication protocols (such as CAN) and control commands.
  • Researchers and students in robotics, autonomous driving and artificial intelligence who need a complete hardware and software reference platform for teaching and research in motion control, SLAM (simultaneous localisation and mapping) and multi-robot coordination.
  • Advanced makers and robotics enthusiasts with solid electronics and programming experience who want to use the Luchs A for their own projects or competitions.
  • Technical support and maintenance engineers who deploy, commission, maintain and troubleshoot the platform, and rely on the hardware description, self-test sequence and fault codes in this manual.

CHAPTER 1Safety

Read before use

Read and understand all safety information in this manual before operating the chassis. Improper use can cause serious injury or damage to equipment.

Prohibited

Environment

  • Do not operate or charge the chassis in rain or snow, in wet conditions, or anywhere it may come into contact with liquids. This can cause short circuits, electric shock or damage.
  • Do not operate the chassis in the presence of flammable, explosive or highly corrosive gases, or in very dusty environments.
  • Do not operate the chassis near sources of strong electromagnetic interference, such as substations or broadcast antennas. Signal loss can cause loss of control.
  • Do not operate or store the chassis outside its operating temperature range of −10 °C to +45 °C.

Operation

  • Do not allow children, untrained persons, or anyone who is tired or under the influence of alcohol or medication to operate the chassis.
  • Do not drive at high speed, or leave the chassis running unattended, near people or obstacles. Always keep the chassis in sight.
  • Do not disassemble or service the chassis, or touch moving or hot parts (such as motors and power electronics), while it is switched on.
  • Do not overload the chassis, exceed its rated speed, or use it for purposes it was not designed for.

Charging

  • Use only the original charger or a charger approved by the manufacturer. An unsuitable power supply can cause fire or explosion.
  • Do not leave the chassis charging unattended for long periods. If the battery swells, changes colour, overheats or smells unusual, stop charging immediately.

Mandatory

Before each use

  • Check that both emergency stop buttons work, that the remote-control transmitter has enough battery, and that the chassis is undamaged.
  • Operate only in an open, level area that is free of obstacles.

Charging and maintenance

  • Charge with the original charger in a dry, well-ventilated place, away from flammable materials.
  • Use only original spare parts. If the chassis will not be used for a long time, charge it regularly and keep the battery at 50–70 % to protect its health.
  • If any fault occurs, switch the chassis off immediately and contact technical support. Do not attempt to dismantle or repair it yourself.

In an emergency

If the chassis goes out of control, catches fire or another emergency occurs:

  1. Press an emergency stop button immediately.
  2. Disconnect the main power.
  3. Follow your emergency plan, move people to safety and deal with the situation.

CHAPTER 2Product overview

2.1 Introduction

The Luchs A is an open mobile robot chassis for research, development, product prototyping and pilot deployments. It is modular, versatile and highly customisable, and supports everything from algorithm validation to full system integration.

Support is available at three levels:

  • Algorithms. The optional navigation kit comes with ROS (Robot Operating System) pre-installed, mainstream SLAM algorithms such as GMapping and Cartographer, and the ROS navigation stack. It supports live mapping, global and local path planning, dynamic obstacle avoidance and trajectory tracking.
  • Applications. Optional interactive software supports online and offline mapping, parameter tuning, data logging and visualisation, making it easy to evaluate algorithms and validate functions.
  • Hardware. The chassis can carry a single-line LiDAR, depth cameras, an IMU (inertial measurement unit) and wheel encoders, and offers a wide range of expansion interfaces for further development and third-party devices.

Compact and complete, the Luchs A is suited to universities, research institutes and companies working on unmanned systems, machine vision and motion control, from teaching and research to early product development.

2.2 Key features

  • Modular, flexible design. Standard mounting interfaces on the body make it quick to add robot arms, lifting modules and other attachments. A dedicated interface for the navigation kit provides a smooth path from basic teaching to advanced research.
  • Comprehensive, layered safety. Ultrasonic obstacle detection, two emergency stops, IP33 protection and a self-test and warning system, plus charging supervision and over-current, over-temperature and short-circuit protection for connected devices.
  • Open hardware and software. Industrial communication interfaces (CAN, RS-232 and RS-485) and high-power 48 V and 12 V outputs give a solid basis for integrating your own devices.

The Luchs A uses a modular architecture: a common main body combined with an interchangeable drive module. The different drive configurations (differential, Ackermann and four-wheel steering) are created by fitting different, interface-compatible drive modules, so the main body and its functions are identical across the range.

Note

The HDMI, USB 2.0 and Ethernet ports (8, 9, 10) are only fitted when the chassis is ordered with the built-in computer.

CHAPTER 3Quick start

Follow these steps to start your Luchs A safely. Before you begin, make sure you have read and understood Chapter 1, Safety.

3.1 Daily check

  1. Walk around the chassis. Check that the area is open, level and clear, the wheels and structure are undamaged, and any load on the rails is secured.
  2. Check the emergency stops. Make sure both emergency stop buttons work and are released.
  3. Check the transmitter. Make sure it has enough battery and that all four toggle switches (SWA–SWD) are up.

3.2 Power on and drive by remote control

  1. Position the chassis. Place it on a level, open indoor floor with no obstacles nearby.
  2. Release the emergency stops. Make sure neither emergency stop button is pressed; otherwise the chassis will not start.
  3. Switch on. Press the power button on the right-hand side of the chassis.
  4. Switch on the transmitter. Move all four toggle switches (SWA–SWD) to the up position, then press and hold both power switches for about 2 seconds until the screen lights up.
  5. Select remote-control mode. Turn the mode selector on the left-hand side of the chassis anticlockwise to the remote-control position. The status lights turn green.
  6. Drive. Use the two sticks on the transmitter to move the chassis. See section 4.3 for details.

3.3 Power off

  1. Stop the chassis and release the sticks. The drive motors hold the chassis in place.
  2. Switch off the chassis by pressing the power button so that it is released. The status lights go dark.
  3. Switch off the transmitter by pressing and holding both power switches until the screen goes dark.

3.4 Charging

  1. Prepare. Place the chassis in a dry, well-ventilated area away from flammable materials.
  2. Connect. Plug the circular connector of the supplied charger firmly into the charging port on the right-hand side of the chassis, then connect the charger to mains power. The charger makes a running noise; this is normal. If the chassis is switched on, the front and rear lights turn orange and the light bar shows charging progress. If it is switched off, the lights stay off.
  3. Finish. When the charger goes quiet, the battery is full. Disconnect the charger from mains power first, then unplug it from the chassis.

A full charge from 0 to 100 % takes about 2 hours with the standard 48 V / 10 A charger.

3.5 Connecting your computer

3.5.1 With the built-in computer

Requires the optional navigation kit with built-in computer.

  1. Connect your devices to the expansion interfaces on the chassis, if you are using any.
  2. Start the system. Place the chassis in a safe area, switch it on and wait for the self-test to finish.
  3. Select automatic mode with the mode selector.
    Safer for debugging: set the mode selector to remote control first, then switch to automatic mode with SWC on the transmitter. In an emergency, flip SWC back to maintenance or remote control to stop the chassis running away.
  4. Connect a display. Connect a monitor to the HDMI port with a standard HDMI cable; the graphical interface appears automatically. If your configuration includes a display, use that instead.
  5. Develop and debug. From the interface you can view system status, sensor data and chassis parameters in real time, write and debug scripts with the built-in tools, and run the SDK examples or call the API to test functions.

3.5.2 With an external computer

  1. Connect your computer and sensors. Connect your industrial PC or edge computer, and any sensors, to the signal port (CAN, RS-232, RS-485) and the expansion power port using the supplied cables.
  2. Start the system. Place the chassis in a safe area, switch it on and wait for the self-test to finish.
  3. Implement the protocol. Choose the protocol for your interface in Chapter 5 and start developing. The ROS software (section 5.4) is a ready-made starting point.

CHAPTER 4Functions in detail

4.1 Power-on self-test

Every time the chassis is switched on, it runs a self-test to make sure the core hardware is working before it can be operated. While the test runs, the status lights fill up in purple. If the test fails, the lights flash red rapidly; contact technical support. The self-test checks the following, in order:

  1. Charging state. The chassis checks whether the charging connector is plugged in. If it is (whether or not charging is in progress), the chassis enters a drive-inhibit state to prevent damage, and ignores the transmitter and the host computer until the connector is removed.
  2. Power system. Battery: checks communication with the BMS (battery management system) and reads battery voltage, temperature and current to confirm they are within safe limits. Power board: checks that each supply rail (such as 12 V and 5 V) is stable.
  3. Communication links. Checks the internal CAN, RS-485 and RS-232 networks.
  4. Motion control. Sends a small test command to each motor driver and confirms through encoder feedback that the motor responds.
  5. Ultrasonic sensors. Sends a test pulse to each sensor and analyses the echo to confirm it is working.

The power button switches the main power of the chassis on and off. It latches in position and has a built-in indicator that is driven directly by the hardware, so it always shows the true supply state.

The emergency stop buttons have the highest priority of all safety devices. Pressing either one cuts drive power in an emergency and brakes the chassis immediately, protecting people and equipment. There is one button on each side of the chassis.

4.3 Remote control

In remote-control mode (mode selector turned anticlockwise) you drive the chassis with the handheld transmitter.

4.3.1 Switching the transmitter on and off

Press and hold the two power switches at the bottom of the transmitter at the same time. The screen lights up when the transmitter is on and goes dark when it is off. The transmitter only switches on when all four toggle switches, SWA to SWD, are in the up position.

4.3.2 Driving

Drive the chassis with the two sticks and the VRB thumbwheel at the top right of the transmitter.

Table 4-5 · Stick functions
ControlMovementA-DFA-FA · A-DAA-4WS
Left stickForward / backForward / reverseForward / reverseForward / reverse
Left stickLeft / rightNo responseNo responseMoves sideways left / right
Right stickLeft / rightPivot turn anticlockwise / clockwiseSteers left / right (Ackermann)Pivot turn anticlockwise / clockwise
VRB thumbwheelLeft / rightPivot turn anticlockwise / clockwisePivot turn anticlockwise / clockwisePivot turn anticlockwise / clockwise
Note

In normal remote-control use the A-4WS drives in four-wheel-steering mode. As soon as it receives a command over CAN or the serial port that selects a specific motion model, remote control switches to that model as well. This makes it easier to check odometry when you are developing autonomous navigation.

4.3.3 Ultrasonic stop and manual override (SWA)

In remote-control mode the ultrasonic sensors constantly watch for obstacles. If an obstacle comes closer than 20 cm, the chassis makes a safety stop and holds its position. Once you have confirmed it is safe, you can override the stop with SWA.

SWD turns the wheels into a parking position in remote-control mode, so that a heavily loaded chassis cannot roll when it is standing on a slope.

4.3.7 Transmitter battery

When the transmitter is on, the TX icon on its screen shows the remaining battery. The transmitter warns you when the battery is low; replace the batteries promptly.

  1. Open the battery cover on the back of the transmitter.
  2. Insert four fully charged AA batteries, making sure the terminals make good contact.
  3. Close the battery cover.

4.4 Control modes

The chassis always knows who is in control, and it, not the host computer, decides which source it accepts. The mode is set with the mode selector on the chassis (section 4.2.3) or, from remote control, with SWC on the transmitter (section 4.3.5).

Table 4-10 · Control modes
ModeHow to enterAcceptsPurpose
Remote controlMode selector anticlockwise, or SWC upTransmitterManual driving, moving the chassis, supervising tests. Status lights green.
AutomaticMode selector clockwise, or SWC downHost computerYour software drives the chassis over CAN, RS-232 or RS-485. Status lights blue.
MaintenanceMode selector in the centre, or SWC centreNeither (SWC only)Commissioning and recovery: errors, including an emergency stop, are cleared here; the parking brake release lets you push the chassis. Status lights yellow.
Remote control always wins

With the mode selector on remote control, flipping SWC up takes control back from the host computer immediately.

4.5 Safety functions

4.5.1 Emergency stop

The emergency stop buttons are the highest-priority safety devices and stop all operation immediately. Pressing either button:

  • cuts the motion-control signals immediately,
  • brakes the drive system, and
  • locks the chassis in a safe state.

To recover:

  1. Make sure the hazard has been removed.
  2. Turn the emergency stop button clockwise to release it.
  3. Turn the mode selector to another position, then back to the original mode.
  4. The system clears the error automatically and resumes normal operation.

4.5.2 Hardware monitoring

The system continuously monitors its key components. If it detects a fault, it stops motion control immediately and flashes the status lights red, so that faults are caught early and isolated. It monitors:

  • motor condition (overload, stall),
  • validity of sensor data,
  • power-module parameters, and
  • communication links.

4.5.3 Battery management (BMS)

The BMS monitors charging, discharging, voltage and temperature. In the event of over-charge, over-discharge, over-current or abnormal temperature, it automatically disconnects power or adjusts the charging current, preventing damage or accidents and extending battery life.

4.5.4 Ultrasonic collision protection

The ultrasonic sensors monitor the surroundings in real time. When an obstacle is closer than 20 cm, the chassis responds according to the operating mode:

  • Remote control: with SWA up, the chassis stops and transmitter commands are ignored; with SWA down, you can override the stop manually.
  • Automatic: the ultrasonic distances are reported in real time over the protocol, and the chassis follows the commands from your navigation system, which fuses this data with its other sensors.

The serial protocols also offer an indoor collision-avoidance setting (30 cm stop distance) and an outdoor setting (50 cm); see Chapter 5.

4.5.5 Charging interlock

As soon as the charging connector is plugged in, whether the chassis is switched on or the charger is powered, the chassis disables the drive (emergency brake and park) and ignores all commands from the transmitter and the host computer. Only the computer power, the expansion power outputs and the charging lights stay on. This prevents the chassis from moving while connected to the charger and ensures safe charging.

4.5.6 Output protection

Every power channel of the chassis has real-time current monitoring with programmable soft cut-off. Critical outputs (drive, navigation and brakes) also have hardware protection against overload, short circuit and over-temperature. If any of these protections trips, restart the chassis.

Two parallel 2040 aluminium extrusions run along the top of the chassis at 200 mm centres. Use standard 40-series slot accessories to mount your own structures or sensor brackets. Ready-made mounting accessories are available on request.

CHAPTER 5Communication interfaces and software

The Luchs A provides three industrial communication interfaces, CAN, RS-485 and RS-232, so you can control the chassis and read its sensor data with your own software. The same definitions are available as spreadsheets: Luchs_A_CAN_Protocol_v1.1.xlsx and Luchs_A_Serial_Protocol_v1.0.xlsx.

Values under confirmation

Fields shaded yellow carry values that are still being confirmed. Check them against live data from your unit before relying on them.

InterfaceUseDocumentation

RS-485 / RS-232Alternative serial controlSection 5.3 · Luchs_A_Serial_Protocol_v1.0.xlsx

The Luchs A protocol uses the same identifiers and layouts as the core frames of the Luchs Chassis Interface (LCI) used on Luchs B, and the ROS software drives both chassis from one code base.

5.2 CAN protocol

StandardCAN 2.0B
Bit rate1 Mbit/s
Frame formatStandard frame, 11-bit identifier, 8-byte payload
Byte orderBig-endian: the high byte of a multi-byte signal is sent first
Physical valueRaw value × factor. Speeds and angles are signed 16-bit integers with a factor of 0.001 (m/s, rad/s, rad).
DirectionsHost → Chassis: commands from your computer. Chassis → Host: feedback from the chassis controller.

5.3 Serial protocols (RS-485 / RS-232)

InterfacesRS-485 and RS-232 on the DB9 signal port under the magnetic cover at the rear of the top plate:
pin 1 = RS-232 RX, pin 2 = RS-232 TX, pin 6 = RS-485 A, pin 7 = RS-485 B, pins 3, 8, 9 = GND
Serial settingsBaud rate: see firmware release notes. Data bits, parity and stop bits: see firmware release notes.
Frame structureHeader byte + payload + tail byte, fixed length per configuration. No length field and no checksum.
Byte orderint16 ("short") values are transmitted high byte first.
ScalingSpeeds and angles: raw = physical value × 1000 (0.001 m/s, 0.001 rad/s, 0.001 rad per bit).
External serial controlCommand byte "External serial control" selects whether the serial port is used for control: 0x01 when an external compute unit drives the chassis, 0x00 when the built-in compute unit is used.

Each configuration uses its own frame header and tail:

ConfigurationCommand headerCommand tailFeedback headerFeedback tailFrame length
Luchs A-DF0xA10x1A0xA20x2A13 bytes
Luchs A-FA, Luchs A-DA0xB10x1B0xB20x2B17 bytes
Luchs A-4WS0xC10x1C0xC20x2C21 bytes

Confirm the frame header and tail against the firmware release shipped with your unit. Some earlier documentation uses 0xA1 / 0x1A (command) and 0xA2 / 0x2A (feedback) for all configurations.

5.4 ROS software

The ROS software for the Luchs family is supplied as luchs_ros2 (version 1.1, ROS 2 Humble and Jazzy) and luchs_ros1 (version 1.1, ROS 1 Noetic). Both are built on the same ROS-independent C++ SDK and drive Luchs A and Luchs B from one code base, with the same topics, frames and services. Publish a velocity on cmd_vel; the driver sends the CAN commands, enforces speed, steering and acceleration limits, and stops the chassis when commands or feedback stop.

Table 5-10 · Packages
PackageContent
luchs_sdkC++ library without ROS: CAN protocols, SocketCAN, steering kinematics, watchdogs, built-in chassis simulators, luchs_cli tool, Python examples
luchs_driverDriver node; parameter files for A-DF, A-FA, A-DA and A-4WS (and Luchs B)
luchs_msgsChassisState, SafetyState, LampCommand, DriveCommand and services
luchs_descriptionRobot model (URDF) for all four configurations, with mounting frames on the rails
luchs_bringup · luchs_teleopLaunch files, CAN set-up script, start-at-boot units, gamepad configuration
Table 5-11 · Main topics of the driver
DirectionTopicTypeContent
Subscribedcmd_velgeometry_msgs/TwistVelocity: forward, sideways (A-4WS), yaw rate
Publishedodomnav_msgs/OdometryWheel odometry and the odom → base_footprint transform
Publishedjoint_statessensor_msgs/JointStateSteering angles and wheel rotation, for the robot model
Published~/state · ~/safetyluchs_msgs/…Chassis state, faults, lamps; emergency stops, bumpers, ultrasonic ranges
Publishedbattery_statesensor_msgs/BatteryStateState of charge, voltage, temperature
Published/diagnosticsdiagnostic_msgs/…Link status, faults, battery warning

Quick start (ROS 2): bring the CAN interface up at 1 Mbit/s (setup_can.sh can0), set the mode selector to automatic, then ros2 launch luchs_bringup luchs_a.launch.py build:=4ws (or df, fa, da). ROS 1: roslaunch luchs_bringup luchs_a.launch build:=4ws. Without a chassis, add dry_run:=true to run against the built-in simulator. The README and the docs folder in each package cover installation, wiring, parameters, sensor integration and troubleshooting.

A few protocol details depend on the chassis firmware release. They are driver parameters (protocol.*); check them once per vehicle as described in docs/protocol_luchs_a.md.

5.5 Autonomy by TAR (option)

The Luchs family is built for autonomy. TerraAgent Robotics (TAR) supplies it as an option: sensor kit, compute, positioning, perception, planning, vehicle control and the control station, integrated on the Luchs A and delivered as one system. TAR software drives the chassis through the interfaces and the ROS driver described in this chapter, so sections 5.1 to 5.4 apply to a vehicle with the TAR kit as well. Figure 5-1 shows building blocks that already run on real vehicles and real data.

  • Positioning degrades safely: RTK, then visual-inertial coasting at reduced speed, then a timed safe stop; LiDAR map localisation is the second source when satellites drop out.
  • Perception is camera-first, with LiDAR and radar added per application: 3D detection, a drivable-ground map and a live elevation map for holes and steps.
  • Planning runs in three layers (route, behaviour, trajectory) and hands its commands to the chassis through the ROS driver.

The functions, the sensor kit and the delivery for your site are agreed with TAR. Contact details are in section 6.3.

CHAPTER 6Maintenance and support

6.1 Routine care

  • Check the wheels, suspension and fasteners before each use.
  • Operate and store the chassis between −10 °C and 45 °C.
  • If the chassis is not used for a long time, keep the battery between 50 % and 70 % and charge it regularly.
  • Use only original spare parts and the supplied charger.
  • If a fault occurs, switch the chassis off and contact support; do not dismantle it yourself.

6.2 Warranty

The warranty terms for your Luchs A are set out in your sales contract with RJ Tech Limited. They exclude normal wear, consumables and damage from misuse, accident or unauthorised modification.

APPENDIX ADimensions

All dimensions in millimetres.

APPENDIX BFault codes

Chassis fault codes are reported in CAN message 0x5B8 (byte 3) and in the fault-status byte of every serial feedback frame. Codes 0x00 to 0x04 appear in the serial protocol only.

CodeMeaning
0x00No fault
0x01Ultrasonic stop triggered
0x02Emergency stop triggered
0x03Parking brake engaged
0x04Charging (charger connected; motion disabled)
0x05Left-front wheel drive fault (left drive on single-motor-per-side builds)
0x06Right-front wheel drive fault (right drive on single-motor-per-side builds)
0x07Left-rear wheel drive fault
0x08Right-rear wheel drive fault
0x09Left-front steering motor fault (front steering motor on single-steering-motor builds)
0x0ARight-front steering motor fault
0x0BLeft-rear steering motor fault
0x0CRight-rear steering motor fault
0x0DRemote-control timeout in remote-control mode (transmitter out of range or switched off)
0x0EWatchdog triggered

APPENDIX CTerms and abbreviations

4WDFour-wheel drive: every wheel has its own drive motor.
4WSFour-wheel steering: every wheel can be steered on its own.
Ackermann steeringCar-style steering in which the inner wheel turns more sharply than the outer one, so both follow the same arc.
BMSBattery Management System: electronics that monitor and protect the battery.
CANController Area Network: a robust two-wire bus widely used in vehicles and machines.
DB99-pin D-subminiature connector.
Host computerThe computer that commands the chassis, such as the built-in computer or your industrial PC.
IMUInertial Measurement Unit: measures acceleration and rotation rate.
IP33Ingress Protection rating to IEC 60529: protected against solid objects over 2.5 mm and against spraying water.
LiFePO4Lithium iron phosphate: a lithium-ion battery chemistry known for long cycle life and thermal stability.
MCUMicrocontroller unit: the main controller of the chassis.
OdometryAn estimate of the robot's motion calculated from wheel speeds and steering angles.
Pivot turnTurning on the spot about the centre of the chassis.
ROSRobot Operating System: widely used open-source robotics middleware.
RS-232 / RS-485Serial communication standards. RS-485 is differential and suits longer, noisier cable runs.
SDKSoftware Development Kit.
SLAMSimultaneous Localisation and Mapping: building a map while working out where the robot is on it.
SocketCANThe standard CAN interface of the Linux kernel.
